Hulking describes something — almost always a person, animal, or object — that is very large, very heavy, and solidly built, in a way that feels physically imposing and somewhat awkward. Think of a body or object that takes up a lot of space, looks heavy and slow, and gives off a sense of raw physical mass.

If you saw a man who was extremely broad, thick, and heavy — built like a boulder more than a person — and his sheer size made him look a little clumsy and difficult to move around, you would call him a hulking man.

This is where "hulking" becomes interesting. It is not a neutral word, and it is not a compliment.

When you call something hulking, you are not just saying it is big. You are saying its size feels excessive, ungainly, and slightly overwhelming. There is a quiet sense that the thing is too large — bulky in a way that feels almost out of place. A hulking figure doesn't move gracefully; it lumbers. A hulking machine doesn't look elegant; it looks brutish and heavy.

Think of the difference between describing a man as strong versus hulking. "Strong" is a compliment. "Hulking" is more like a description of raw, heavy, almost clumsy mass. It is said with a kind of awe, but not admiration. It is closer to saying this thing is big in a way that feels almost too much.

Hulking is most commonly used to describe:

People, especially men. A hulking bodyguard, a hulking wrestler, a hulking stranger standing in a doorway. The word almost always points to someone whose sheer physical bulk feels intimidating or overpowering.

Animals. A hulking bear, a hulking gorilla — creatures whose size and heaviness make them look powerful but slow.

Man-made objects and structures. A hulking factory, a hulking truck, a hulking warship. When applied to things, it means the object is massive and heavy-looking in an unrefined, industrial way — not elegant, not sleek, but big and looming.

This is very important for using the word correctly.

Hulking does not simply mean tall. A very tall, thin person is not hulking. The word is really about bulk and heaviness, not height alone.

Hulking does not mean muscular in an attractive way. If you want to say someone looks athletic and powerful in a flattering sense, words like muscular, athletic, or built are more appropriate. Hulking suggests heavy mass, not lean strength.

Hulking does not mean strong. A person can be hulking without being particularly strong. It is about how they look, not what they can do.

Hulking is not a compliment. Even when used without any obvious insult, the word always carries a slight edge — it implies the kind of bigness that is imposing rather than admirable.

Here are examples that show the word in action across different contexts:

  • The security guard was a hulking man who barely fit through the doorway.
    → He was so large and heavy-set that he seemed almost too big for a normal space.
  • A hulking figure appeared at the end of the dark alley.
    → The person was massive and looming, which felt threatening.
  • The old factory was a hulking building of rusted steel and broken windows.
    → The factory was enormous and heavy-looking, but rundown and unrefined.
  • The bear rose to its full height — a hulking beast that towered over the hiker.
    → The bear was massive and heavy, inspiring fear.
  • He had been a hulking teenager, always tripping over his own feet.
    → He was heavily built and large, but in a clumsy, awkward way.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Several words are close to "hulking" but each means something slightly different. Understanding these differences will make your use of "hulking" precise.

Massive just means very large. It is neutral and has no connotation of clumsiness or awkwardness. A beautiful mountain can be massive. Nothing can be beautifully hulking.

Huge simply means very large in size. Again, neutral. "Hulking" always implies heavy bulk and a slightly negative or imposing quality that "huge" does not.

Burly means large, heavy, and strong — and is often used almost admiringly. A burly man is big and tough in a way that can seem capable and reliable. A hulking man is big and heavy in a way that seems overpowering and awkward.

Bulky means taking up a lot of space in an unwieldy way. It focuses on the inconvenience of size. "Hulking" is more vivid and more focused on the visual impression of imposing, heavy mass.

Lumbering describes the movement of something heavy and slow. A hulking man might move in a lumbering way, but "hulking" itself describes how something looks, not how it moves.
Register — When and Where Is This Word Used?

"Hulking" is an informal to semi-formal word. You will find it comfortably in:

Everyday conversation, novels and fiction, newspaper writing, and general non-academic writing. It brings colour and vividness to descriptions, making them feel alive rather than flat.

You would not typically use "hulking" in formal academic or scientific writing, where precise and neutral language is preferred.

If you ever need to recall the meaning instantly: hulking means so large, heavy, and solidly built that it looks imposing, ungainly, and almost too big for its surroundings — with the quiet suggestion that this kind of size is not graceful or elegant, but raw and overwhelming.
